slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open the lecture by positioning the appendix as a small but powerful tool rather than a side calculation. The central question is what an orthogonal symmetry group can preserve when its action refuses to split the ambient vector space into smaller stable pieces.

slides.title: Lecture Map
slides.notes: Present the appendix as a dependency map. The same commutant idea controls both conclusions: first it limits invariant symmetric bilinear forms, then it limits the possible center and closure behavior of the connected Lie subgroup.

slides.title: Irreducibility
slides.notes: Pause on the word irreducible, because it is the hypothesis doing the work. The action may have many orbits, but it cannot leave a smaller linear coordinate block stable, so any construction producing such a block contradicts the setup.

slides.title: Commutant
slides.notes: Explain that every later argument begins with an operator commuting with the group. Once the operator commutes, its kernels, images, and polynomial eigenspaces are also respected by the group, so irreducibility turns linear algebra into a severe dichotomy.

slides.title: Lemma 1
slides.notes: Use this slide to make Lemma 1 feel concrete. The proof does not classify all representations; it classifies the algebra seen by a single commuting operator. Irreducibility removes nilpotent and split-polynomial possibilities before they can grow.

slides.title: Splitting Obstruction
slides.notes: This is the proof move students should remember. A factorization is not merely a symbolic event; through the kernels of the factors it tries to create an invariant direct sum. Irreducibility rejects that picture unless one side is trivial.

slides.title: Lemma 2 Symmetric
slides.notes: Emphasize the geometric meaning of the symmetric case. A self-adjoint commuting operator would encode a new invariant ellipsoid. Lemma 2 says irreducibility and orthogonality round that ellipsoid into a scalar multiple of the original metric.

slides.title: Skew Case
slides.notes: The skew-symmetric part explains why a one-dimensional center can appear later. A nonzero skew operator behaves like multiplication by the imaginary unit on paired planes, and the irreducibility argument prevents two independent such rotations from coexisting.

slides.title: Theorem 1
slides.notes: Walk through Theorem 1 as a three-line proof with a lot of meaning. The only representation theorem needed is the commutant lemma; once the form is represented by a symmetric operator, invariant geometry becomes scalar linear algebra.

slides.title: Holonomy Use
slides.notes: Connect the algebra back to geometry. At a point, holonomy acts by orthogonal transformations on the tangent space. Parallel tensors are exactly the objects transported consistently around loops, so Theorem 1 says irreducible holonomy leaves no new symmetric tensor beyond the metric scale.

slides.title: Theorem 2
slides.notes: State Theorem 2 without making it sound automatic. A connected Lie subgroup of a compact group need not be visibly closed from its parametrization. The proof shows that irreducibility eliminates the extra closure directions that could otherwise appear.

slides.title: Center
slides.notes: This slide is the bridge between the two theorems. The skew-operator conclusion from Lemma 2 returns as a statement about the center of the Lie algebra. There is room for no center, or for one circle of rotations, but not for a larger torus.

slides.title: Semisimple Part
slides.notes: Keep the Lie algebra notation simple. The invariant trace inner product lets the proof take orthogonal complements without losing ideal structure. Once the center is isolated, the remaining part splits into simple pieces that behave semisimply.

slides.title: Closure Argument
slides.notes: Do not overload the audience with every historical reference. The main mechanism is that a hypothetical extra closure direction acts on each complex irreducible summand as a scalar. Semisimplicity supplies trace zero, forcing every such scalar to vanish.

slides.title: Reducible Contrast
slides.notes: Use the contrast to protect students from overgeneralizing Theorem 1. If the representation splits, each stable block can carry its own scale. Irreducibility is exactly what removes those independent weights and forces a single scalar.

slides.title: Instructor Board
slides.notes: This slide turns the appendix into a reusable classroom checklist. For any proposed holonomy or symmetry example, first test reducibility, then inspect commuting operators, and finally translate the result into metric uniqueness or the possible circle in the center.

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the main course narrative. The appendix is short because the idea is focused: irreducibility shrinks the commutant. That shrinking explains metric uniqueness for irreducible holonomy and gives closedness needed for Lie-group arguments.
